body:
The disciples are hungry. They pick heads of grain, rub them between their fingers, and eat. It is such a small detail that we might wonder why Luke even mentions it. But that movement of their hands is exactly what the Pharisees notice. To them, rubbing the grain could be considered work on the Sabbath.

And suddenly I wonder how often we do the same thing.

They were watching the disciples’ fingers while God Himself was walking beside them.

The Pharisees were not wrong to care about the Sabbath. It was sacred. Their mistake was allowing their understanding of the law to become so consuming that they could no longer recognize the One the law was pointing toward.

Jesus reminds them of David eating the sacred bread when he and his companions were hungry. Then He says something astonishing: “The Son of Man is lord of the sabbath.”

Perhaps one of the greatest dangers in our spiritual lives is not always doing something obviously wrong. Sometimes it is becoming so certain that we are right that we stop looking for God.

We can know Scripture and still miss its heart. We can defend our beliefs and forget compassion. We can notice another person’s smallest failure while remaining completely unaware of what God may be doing in that person’s life. We can become so occupied with the grain between someone’s fingers that we fail to see Christ standing beside them.

And perhaps this Gospel asks an uncomfortable question:

What am I watching so closely that I might be missing Jesus?

The rules mattered. The Sabbath mattered. But mercy mattered too. The Pharisees saw a violation. Jesus saw hungry men.

Maybe faith requires more than knowing what is right. It requires a heart close enough to God to understand why it is right.
prayer: Lord, protect me from a faith that sees everything except You. When I become quick to judge, slow me down. When I am convinced that I am right, keep my heart humble. Give me eyes that notice the person before the fault, mercy before judgment, and above all, Your presence in the ordinary moments I so easily overlook. Amen.
title: When Being Right Makes Us Blind

body:
There are things about ourselves we carry for so long that we hardly recognize them anymore. Ways of protecting ourselves, avoiding what frightens us, controlling what we can, retreating when we feel inadequate. Eventually they can become so familiar that we simply think, This is who I am.

Jesus says today that new wine cannot be poured into old wineskins. The new wine is the life He brings, and receiving it requires something within us willing to stretch. Yet Jesus also understands our resistance: “No one who has been drinking old wine desires new, for he says, ‘The old is good.’” We cling to what is familiar, even when God may be trying to lead us somewhere new.

I recognize this in myself. When I feel uncertain, especially around someone stronger, more confident, or more articulate, something in me wants to retreat. I would rather quietly find another way than risk saying what I need to say. Perhaps some of these patterns began long ago. They protected me once, but that does not mean they must continue to define me.

And then Paul reminds us not to judge too quickly, even ourselves. God will reveal what is hidden and “manifest the motives of our hearts.” That can sound frightening, but perhaps it is actually mercy. God already sees beneath the behavior—to the fear, the wounds, the good intentions, the failures, and the sincere desire to love Him.

Maybe we don’t need to ask God not to see those hidden places.

Maybe we need to pray, Lord, see all the way through me.

At whatever age we find ourselves, we are not finished. There is still something God can heal, something He can teach us, some old wineskin He can gently stretch or replace. We are not captive to the ways we have always responded.

Perhaps conversion sometimes looks very ordinary: staying when we would normally retreat, speaking when we would normally become silent, surrendering an outcome we would normally try to control, and trusting God enough to enter something unfamiliar.

The old may feel safer. But Christ is still offering new wine.
prayer: Lord, You already know everything I try to hide, even from myself. See all the way through me. Heal what still needs healing and loosen my grip on the things I try to control. Give me courage to leave behind the patterns that keep me captive. Make my heart flexible enough to receive whatever new thing You are doing in me. I trust You with what comes next. Amen.
title: New Wine, Old Wineskins

body:
By the time Jesus steps into Simon’s boat, people are already pressing toward Him. They have heard Him teach, witnessed His healings, and are searching for Him. Simon himself has already encountered Jesus—he watched Him enter his home and heal his mother-in-law. So when Jesus asks him to take the boat into deeper water, Simon knows there is something different about this man. Still, he is a fisherman who has worked through the night and caught nothing. He is tired, his nets are already being washed, and experience tells him there are no fish to be caught. Yet he answers, “At your command I will lower the nets.”

What follows is abundance beyond anything Simon could have produced himself. The nets begin to tear and the boats nearly sink. But Simon hardly seems interested in the fish anymore. Something much greater has happened: he recognizes who is standing before him. “Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man.” Jesus does not depart. He tells him, “Do not be afraid.” Then He calls Simon, James, and John to follow Him.

Perhaps that is what makes this Gospel so beautiful. Jesus does not wait for Simon to become Peter, the great Apostle. He calls him while he is still becoming—tired, uncertain, aware of his shortcomings, and unable to understand where any of this will lead.

And maybe “put out into deep water” is still Christ’s invitation to us. There are places in our lives where we have tried, failed, grown tired, or simply stopped expecting anything more. Christ does not always explain what He is doing. Sometimes He simply asks us to trust Him enough to lower the nets once more.

We may not know what waits in the deeper water. We only know Who is asking us to go.
title: At Your Command
prayer: Lord, when I am tired, uncertain, or afraid to try again, give me the faith to say, “At Your command, I will go.” Lead me into the deeper places where I cannot depend only upon myself, and help me trust that You already know what waits there. Amen.

body:
Paul was watching something extraordinary happen. The first Christian communities were beginning to blossom, but they were still filled with very human people. They divided themselves, followed personalities, questioned one another, and sometimes lost sight of Christ. Paul continually reminded them: I am only a servant. We are all instruments. God alone gives the growth.

How remarkable that after two thousand years, we are not so different.

Christian communities have multiplied across the world, yet the human heart still struggles with the same things. We divide, misunderstand, wander away, return, and try again. And somehow, despite us, God continues to give the growth. Perhaps perseverance itself is one of His quiet gifts.

Then Jesus tells us exactly why He has come: “I must proclaim the good news of the Kingdom of God, because for this purpose I have been sent.”

The crowds want Him to remain with them, but He cannot stay in one place. The Kingdom must keep moving outward—to another town, another person, another generation. Eventually it moved through Paul, through those imperfect early communities, through countless generations of believers, until somehow it reached us.

That thought makes Christ feel remarkably close.

We did not walk beside Him through Galilee. We did not hear His human voice or watch Him heal the sick. Yet the Kingdom He proclaimed that morning is still being proclaimed today. We are living inside the continuation of something He began.

And perhaps we are still imperfect instruments through which He carries it forward.
title: The Kingdom Is Still Blossoming
prayer: Lord, remain close to me. When I wander, draw me back. When I cannot see You, help me recognize the traces of Your grace around me. Let me feel Your warmth and direction, and use even my imperfect life for Your purpose. Your Kingdom is still growing. Let something of it grow through me. Amen.

body:
There is a place within us that no other person can completely reach. We can explain ourselves, share our thoughts, even give someone our whole history—and still there remains an interior depth known only to us.

Paul begins there today and then takes us somewhere almost beyond comprehension: just as our own spirit knows what lies within us, only the Spirit of God knows the depths of God. And that Spirit has been given to us.

Think about what that means.

The Holy Spirit is not merely our conscience, an emotion, or that quiet feeling we sometimes experience in prayer. He is God. The Spirit who knows the very depths of God chooses, through grace, to dwell within the human person.

Perhaps this is why there are moments when Scripture suddenly opens before us, when separate words somehow become connected, when something touches the heart before the mind can fully explain it. We should never mistake every feeling for the voice of God, yet neither should we dismiss the possibility that God is quietly teaching us from within.

Paul takes it even further: “Who has known the mind of the Lord, so as to counsel him?” No one stands above God. No human wisdom can instruct Him. And yet Paul follows with the extraordinary words: “But we have the mind of Christ.”

Not because we have figured God out, but because His Spirit is slowly teaching us to see differently—to recognize truth, to desire what is good, to love more deeply, to become more like Christ.

Then the Gospel shows us the opposite. An unclean spirit inhabits a man and even recognizes Jesus. But recognition is not communion. At Christ’s simple command—“Be quiet! Come out of him!”—it must leave. Evil has a voice, but it does not have the final authority. Christ does.

There is something humbling in all of this. The God who towers beyond everything we could ever understand does not remain distant. He pours His grace into the deepest places of the human person and asks us to make room for Him.

Maybe the spiritual life is not about trying harder to reach a distant God.

Maybe it begins by becoming quiet enough to discover that He has already come near.

Pray
prayer: Holy Spirit, quiet everything within me that keeps me from recognizing You. Teach me to distinguish Your movement from my own desires and fears. Enter the places in me no one else can reach, and form within me the mind of Christ. May Your grace move through my thoughts, my words, and my life, until there is more of You and less of what keeps me from You. Amen.
title: “We have the mind of Christ”
theme: Do you know the mind of Christ?

body:
There is something difficult in today’s Gospel. Jesus stands among people who have known Him for years, yet they cannot recognize what God is doing right before them. Then He speaks of the widow of Zarephath and Naaman the Syrian—outsiders whom God chose to receive His grace. It angered them because God was not acting according to their expectations.

Perhaps that is what stayed with me: God’s presence and purpose do not always appear where, or how, we expect them to.

Last night I was reading about Dolly Parton and was touched by something she has often expressed—that her gifts came from God and were meant to be used for His glory. There was something about that simple recognition, and the joy with which she seems to live it, that made me reflect upon my own life.

Not whether I have done as much, but whether I have truly recognized God in what I have been given.

There comes a time when we begin to look differently at the years behind us and more carefully at the years still ahead. I know I have been given gifts. I know I have tried to use them, sometimes graciously and sometimes imperfectly. But now the desire feels different. I don’t want merely to use what God has given me. I want my life to belong to Him.

Maybe that is part of what this Gospel asks of us—to stop deciding beforehand where God should be found and begin noticing where He already is. Perhaps He has been present in our gifts, our ordinary encounters, our disappointments, even in the restless longing that tells us there must be something more.

And perhaps that longing itself is grace.

I cannot change the years already lived. But I can ask that whatever time remains becomes more conscious of Him, more available to Him, and somehow more capable of carrying His light.
prayer: Lord, open my eyes to the ways You have always been present in my life. Take the gifts You have given me and the time still before me. Teach me to live them with joy and for Your glory. Above all, draw me nearer to You, until Your light becomes visible through mine. Amen.
title: Glorify God by your life…… that was Dolly Parton’s mission

body:
The beheading of John the Baptist is difficult to read. A life is taken so easily, almost casually, because of pride, anger and the pressure of a room full of people. Yet what strikes me is that Herod actually liked listening to John. John perplexed him. Herod knew there was something righteous and holy about him, and when the request came for John’s head, he was deeply distressed. He didn’t really want to kill him. But he had made his boast in front of his guests, and apparently admitting he was wrong was more unbearable than committing an act he knew was wrong.

Then Paul’s words become almost painfully clear: “Whoever boasts, should boast in the Lord.” Herod had the palace, the title, the banquet and the authority, while John had nothing but a prison cell. Yet who was really free? John could speak the truth without needing anyone’s approval. Herod had all the power in the room and was controlled by what everyone in that room might think of him.

Maybe this is why God chooses the weak, the lowly and those the world considers nothing. They reveal how little worldly power actually means. Herodias could silence John, but she could not make his words untrue. Herod could take his life, but he could not take what John belonged to.

Our own banquets may look different. Pride can still trap us into defending something we know is wrong simply because admitting the truth would cost us our image. Perhaps today’s question is not whether I am strong enough to stand like John. It is much simpler: When truth and my pride collide, which one am I willing to surrender?
title: Who Is Really Free?
prayer: Lord, give me the humility to boast only in You, and the courage to choose what is right even when it costs me something.
theme: Herod, if asked again, would you do it?

title: When there are no doors...
body:
I want so badly to do the will of God. That should bring peace, shouldn't it? Instead, I feel restless. I keep asking Him what I am supposed to do, where I am supposed to go, what I am missing. I look for some movement, some opening, some indication that I am headed in the right direction. Nothing. I run into walls. There are no doors.

So I do what I always do. I start thinking. And then I think about my thinking. Are my intentions pure? Am I trusting God or manipulating things because I am afraid of an outcome I cannot control? Did I push too hard? Did I not push hard enough? Am I supposed to wait? Have I waited too long? My mind can take one unanswered question and turn it into twenty.

And into that comes Paul: *Christ did not send me to baptize but to preach the Gospel, and not with the wisdom of human eloquence, so that the cross of Christ might not be emptied of its meaning.* Then: *I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the learning of the learned I will set aside.*

Maybe I cannot think my way to God.

That is difficult for me to accept because thinking feels like doing something. If I can analyze every possibility, perhaps I can prevent the wrong one. If something makes me uncomfortable, I can adjust it, push it, fix it, manipulate it just enough to make the outcome feel safer. Except then I have changed the outcome myself. I cannot leave well enough alone because I am terrified of the empty space. And right now there is a lot of empty space.

What do you do when you want your life to belong to God but you don't know what He wants you to do with it? What does faithfulness look like when you are sitting in your house, without direction, without some great opportunity waiting for you, without anyone telling you that what you are doing matters?

Then Jesus tells the story of ten virgins waiting for the bridegroom. Waiting. That word suddenly looks different to me. The wise ones were not out accomplishing something extraordinary when the bridegroom came. They were simply prepared. They had oil for their lamps.

Maybe I have confused preparation with accomplishment. Maybe I have believed that being ready for God means finding my purpose, doing something meaningful, making an impression, serving in some recognizable way. But what if the oil is something quieter? What if the oil is remaining with God when I cannot hear Him? Praying when prayer gives me no answer. Doing the next good thing without needing to know what it will become. Allowing something uncertain to remain uncertain instead of grabbing hold of it and trying to control the ending. Loving the person who happens to be in front of me. Believing that a day nobody notices can still be a day lived for God.

That is hard for me. God, I want Your comfort. I want some part of You that I can feel and recognize because sometimes the thoughts inside me become so loud that I feel as though I am imploding. I am afraid of wasting my life. I am afraid of missing You. And underneath all of it is a fear I don't particularly want to admit: What if I arrive at the end and discover that I got it wrong?

But perhaps today You are not asking me to figure out my life. Perhaps You are asking me to keep the lamp burning.

So today I will try something different. I will not ask You to show me the whole road. I will stop looking for a door where there isn't one yet. When my mind begins constructing ten different futures, I will come back to the one life actually happening in front of me. I will pray. I will do the good that is mine to do today. I will leave one thing alone that I desperately want to control. And when the emptiness makes me believe that nothing is happening, I will remember the virgins sitting in the darkness with their lamps.

They were waiting, but they were not doing nothing. They were waiting for Someone.

Maybe that is enough for today.

Lord, I don't know where You are taking me. I don't even know what You are doing with me. But I am still here. Keep my lamp burning until I can see You coming.
opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always

body:
There is something almost urgent in Jesus’ words. Not frightening, but deeply personal. As if He is saying: Do not sleep through your own life. Do not become so distracted, discouraged, or distant that you stop noticing Me.

We often hear “stay awake” and think Jesus is warning us to be ready for the end. And He is. But perhaps He is also asking us to be awake to Him right now—in the ordinary moments, in the questions we carry, in the places where faith has grown quiet.

Then Paul gives us the words we need to hear beside Jesus’ warning:

“He will keep you firm to the end… God is faithful.”

That changes everything.

Jesus calls us to remain awake, but He does not leave us to hold everything together by ourselves. We may wander. We may become distracted. We may question God, become disappointed with the Church, or simply stop praying. There may even come a time when we wonder whether we still believe at all.

But our weakness does not change who God is.

God is faithful.

Perhaps some of us have spent so much time wondering whether we still have enough faith in God that we have forgotten to ask whether God still has hold of us.

He does.

If you have stepped away, these readings are not a threat telling you that you had better hurry back before it is too late. They may be something much gentler:

Wake up. Listen. Something in you is still searching.

The fact that you are wondering about God may itself be evidence that the conversation between you and Him is not finished.

Coming back does not require having every question answered. It does not require suddenly becoming the person you once were. It may begin with something much smaller: turning toward Him again and saying, I’m listening.

Jesus says, Stay awake.

And when we wonder whether we can possibly remain faithful enough, Paul answers:

God is faithful.

Maybe that is where we begin.
title: Stay Awake—God Is Still Faithful
Reflection
body:
Maybe you stepped away from the Church because somewhere along the way, you expected it to look different.

Perhaps you saw hypocrisy. People who spoke about Christ but did not seem to live like Him. Maybe you were disappointed by someone in the Church, frustrated by rules you didn’t understand, or simply began to wonder whether any of it was real.

Today’s reading from 2 Thessalonians reminds us of something we sometimes forget: the Church has never been filled with perfect people.

Paul was writing to one of the earliest Christian communities, and already there were problems. People weren’t doing what they should. Some were allowing others to carry their responsibilities. There was disorder and frustration. Paul had to correct them.

This was happening almost from the beginning.

And yet Paul didn’t abandon the Church because some Christians weren’t living as they should. He called them back to what they had been taught. He showed them another way by the way he lived his own life.

Perhaps there is something here for those of us who have walked away.

If someone in the Church disappointed you, that person was never the reason Christ called you in the first place.

If you encountered hypocrisy, Christ is still Christ.

If you stopped practicing because faith began to feel empty, confusing, or disconnected from your life, perhaps you don’t need to have everything figured out before coming back.

The earliest Christians certainly didn’t.

Christianity was never meant to be something we simply receive. Paul tells us through his example that faith asks something of us. We participate. We serve. We carry one another. We struggle, sometimes fail, get corrected, and begin again.

And then, after all Paul’s correction, he ends with something remarkably gentle:

“May the Lord of peace himself give you peace at all times and in every way.”

Maybe that is the invitation today.

Not, Why did you leave?

Not, Why haven’t you come back?

Simply: Come and look again.

Not at every imperfect person who has ever represented the Church poorly.

Look again at Christ.

He is still there.

When Faith Became Something Else

Sometimes we don’t walk away from God.
We walk away from what we thought God had become.

Maybe faith began to feel like obligation. Rules. Judgment. People telling us what we should believe or how we should live. Maybe we saw hypocrisy in people who spoke about God but seemed to have very little mercy for anyone around them.

And somewhere along the way, we stopped coming.

Today’s Gospel is worth hearing if that has ever been you.

Because Jesus saw it too.

He looked directly at the religious leaders of His time and said:

“You have neglected the weightier things of the law: judgment and mercy and fidelity.”

They were doing the religious things. They knew the rules. They observed the smallest requirements of the law.

But Jesus looked beneath all of it and asked: What happened to your heart?

That matters.

Because sometimes the very things that have caused people to turn away from religion are things Jesus Himself condemned.

Hypocrisy bothered Him.
Self-righteousness bothered Him.
Religion without mercy bothered Him.

He wasn’t asking people to abandon faith because of it. He was calling them back to what faith was supposed to be.

And perhaps He still is.

In the first reading, Paul speaks to people who are confused and unsettled. His words are simple: “Stand firm.” Don’t allow every voice, every disappointment, every frightening moment to separate you from what you once knew.

Maybe you aren’t standing very firmly right now.

Maybe you haven’t been inside a church for years. Maybe you’re not even certain what you believe anymore. Maybe something happened that made you decide you wanted nothing more to do with it.

But perhaps the fact that you are still wondering about God means the story isn’t finished.

Jesus never asked us simply to make the outside of the cup look clean. He wanted the inside transformed.

Mercy.
Faithfulness.
Justice.
Love.

This is the Christ who is still there beneath everything that may have disappointed you.

And maybe returning doesn’t begin with suddenly believing everything again. Maybe it begins much smaller.

A prayer you haven’t said in years.

Walking through the doors of a church and sitting quietly in the back.

Asking God one honest question:

“Are You still there?”

And perhaps His answer has been waiting all along:

I never left. Come and see.
title: When Faith becomes something else

body:
He Saw Us Before We Came

How many times have we quietly asked God for proof?

Proof that He is there. Proof that He hears us. Proof that He sees what we are going through. We may believe, we may pray, we may even faithfully seek Him—and still somewhere within us there is that longing: Lord, show me that You are really here.

Nathanael seems to understand this longing.

When Philip tells him that they have found the one spoken of by Moses and the prophets—Jesus of Nazareth—Nathanael’s response is hardly one of immediate faith: “Can anything good come from Nazareth?”

He doubts before he even comes.

Yet when Jesus sees Nathanael approaching, He does something unexpected. He does not chastise him for his skepticism. Instead, He affirms him: “Here is a true child of Israel. There is no duplicity in him.”

Perhaps Jesus recognizes something important in Nathanael. His doubt is real, but so is his honesty. He isn’t pretending to believe something he doesn’t yet understand.

And then Jesus tells him, “Before Philip called you, I saw you under the fig tree.”

We don’t know what happened beneath that tree. We don’t know what Nathanael had been thinking, praying, questioning, or carrying there. But Nathanael knew.

And suddenly it was enough.

“Rabbi, you are the Son of God; you are the King of Israel.”

Maybe this is what so many of us are searching for when we ask God for a sign. We want to know that He sees us beneath our own fig tree—the place no one else knows about. The worry we haven’t spoken aloud. The question we are afraid to ask. The disappointment, loneliness, confusion, or hope hidden within us.

We want to know: Lord, were You there? Did You see me? Do You know me?

And today’s Psalm gives us an answer:

“The LORD is near to all who call upon him, to all who call upon him in truth.”

In truth.

Perhaps that is the invitation.

We don’t have to come to God with perfect faith. Nathanael certainly didn’t. We don’t have to hide our questions or manufacture certainty we don’t possess. We simply have to come wanting Him and willing to call upon Him in truth.

Because before Nathanael ever walked toward Jesus, Jesus had already seen Nathanael.

And before we call upon Him, He has already seen us too.

Maybe faith does not always begin with certainty. Sometimes it begins with simply turning toward Christ and saying, Here I am. I don’t understand everything. I still have questions. But I want to know You.

And Jesus says to Nathanael, “You will see greater things than this.”

Perhaps He says the same to us.

Come.

Call upon Him in truth.

And trust that the One you are searching for has already seen you beneath the fig tree.
title: Come !

opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
title: “And what do we have? History. Where is He?”
body:
Peter saw Him. He walked beside Him, heard His voice, watched Him heal, ate with Him, followed Him from place to place. And what do we have? History. Sometimes I find myself wondering: Where is He?

I have been troubled these past few days. Restless and on edge. I want so badly to see what is good. I want to express love and understanding. I want to recognize the gifts God has placed before me and see Him in the people I encounter and in the ordinary transactions of my life.

Yet sometimes I don't.

Sometimes I see everything through a version of myself I don't particularly want to be. I become frustrated. I judge. I look around at things that need fixing, disorganized things, things I should be doing, and I don't have the energy to change them. I know God is here, and yet there are moments when He feels terribly difficult to see.

Then today I read the Gospel.

Jesus turns to His disciples and asks, “Who do people say that the Son of Man is?” They give Him the answers they have heard. John the Baptist. Elijah. Jeremiah. One of the prophets.

But then Jesus changes the question.

“But who do you say that I am?”

Why did He ask them this?

Perhaps because there comes a point when knowing what everyone else says about God is no longer enough. They had followed Jesus. They had watched Him. They had listened to Him. Now they had to decide for themselves who was standing before them.

Peter answers, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.”

What strikes me is that Peter knew who Jesus was before he understood what Jesus was doing.

Almost immediately afterward, Jesus begins telling the disciples about the suffering and death that await Him, and Peter cannot accept it. The very man who has just declared Jesus to be the Christ still doesn't understand God's plan.

Maybe that is where I find some comfort today.

We can know who God is without understanding what God is doing.

I keep returning to the Old Testament and seeing this again and again. God speaks to His prophets. Kings rise and fall. Things are given, and things are taken away. People obey and disobey, understand and misunderstand. Generations pass, and human beings continue circling the same questions.

And here we are more than two thousand years after Christ walked among us, still asking them.

What is our purpose?

What is God doing?

Why this?

Why now?

Where is He?

I sometimes imagine that faith would have been easier if I had been there. If I could have seen Jesus standing in front of me, surely I would have understood.

But Peter was there.

And Peter still didn't understand.

He saw Jesus and misunderstood Him. He promised loyalty and later denied knowing Him. He became frightened. He failed. And still Jesus chose him.

Maybe seeing isn't the answer I think it is.

Maybe Jesus' question to Peter continues through every generation and eventually reaches each of us:

“But who do you say that I am?”

Perhaps we answer that question over and over throughout our lives.

When life is beautiful, who do you say that I am?

When something is taken from you, who do you say that I am?

When you are grateful, who do you say that I am?

When you are angry, exhausted, disappointed, or unable to understand what is happening around you, who do you say that I am?

Maybe faith isn't reaching some perfect place where we see God in absolutely everything and never become discouraged again.

Maybe faith is returning.

Peter returned.

And perhaps that is why there is something so beautiful about Jesus choosing this imperfect man as His rock.

So where is Christ now?

I wish some days that I could answer that as easily as Peter could by simply pointing across the road.

But perhaps today I don't need to see everything clearly. Perhaps I don't even need to understand.

I only need enough faith to answer the question.

You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.

And when I cannot feel His presence, when the world becomes too loud, and my own thoughts become louder still, perhaps my prayer can simply be:
prayer: Jesus, I know who You are. I just can't see You very well today. Stay with me until I can.

opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
title: Memorial of the Queenship of the Blessed Virgin Mary
body:
Today while reading the Gospel, I had a profound feeling come over me. Jesus warns the crowds about the scribes and Pharisees. He tells them to listen to what they teach, but not to follow their example, because they preach what they do not practice. They place heavy burdens on others but will not lift a finger to help carry them. They seek recognition, titles, important seats and the admiration of others.

And I thought, if there were ever a warning meant for our time, as much as it was meant for theirs, this is it.

We are climbing over one another instead of offering a hand. We are constantly trying to elevate ourselves, or we become enamored with those we have elevated above us. We admire fame, wealth, beauty, power, titles, influence and success until admiration quietly becomes something much closer to worship.

Respecting another human being is one thing. Praising and idolizing them is another.

Why do we do this? What are we searching for?

A quarterback is not your Christ. A television personality is not your teacher of truth simply because millions listen to them. A musician, politician, celebrity, billionaire or person with an impressive title does not possess a soul more valuable than yours. We are earthly brothers and sisters, and somewhere along the way we have forgotten that.

There are no lesser souls.

Jesus says, “The greatest among you must be your servant.” Think about how radically different that is from the world we have created. We measure greatness by who has the most, who commands the room, who gets recognized, who has influence and who sits in the seat of honor. Jesus measures greatness by who is willing to serve.

We need to level the field again.

Racism, poverty, extreme divisions of wealth and status, superiority, contempt and idolatry continue to separate us. We are a torn society, and strangely, we continue craving the very things that tear us apart. We want to belong to the right group, follow the right person, have the right title and stand on the right side of some imaginary line separating “us” from “them.”

But Jesus keeps bringing us back to humility.

Maybe we need to start seeing one another differently—not by status, appearance, profession, politics, money, education or usefulness, but by recognizing the soul standing in front of us.

That means quieting that immediate voice that tells us not to bother with someone. Reach out to your neighbor. Speak to the woman standing beside you in line. Acknowledge the man pumping gas next to you. Be patient with the stranger at Costco. Check on the annoying elderly woman down the street. Look at people long enough to remember that there is an entire human life behind the face you see.

We don't have to agree with everyone. We don't have to admire everyone. But we must stop deciding that some human beings are worth more than others.

There is something especially powerful in Jesus' final words: **“Whoever exalts himself will be humbled; but whoever humbles himself will be exalted.”**

Perhaps we have spent too much time looking sideways—comparing ourselves with one another—and looking upward toward people we have placed on pedestals.

Look higher.

Honor the One who made you.

Let God guide you, not man.

And if you are going to look down, let it only be because you are reaching for the hand of someone who needs help getting back up.

**The only One above us is God. The rest of us belong beside one another.**

title: Readings for the Memorial of Saint Pius X, Pope
body:
Today I read Ezekiel 37:1–14 and Matthew 22:34–40, and at first I struggled to understand how these readings belonged together. Ezekiel can be difficult for me. God continually calls him “son of man,” he experiences these extraordinary visions, and sometimes I find myself wondering what exactly I am supposed to take from all of it.

But today I learned something important. When God calls Ezekiel “son of man,” He is reminding him that he is human. He is mortal. Ezekiel may be standing in the presence of God and receiving incredible visions, but he is still a man who cannot possibly understand everything God understands.

Then God brings Ezekiel into a valley filled with dry bones and asks him, “Son of man, can these bones live?”

Ezekiel gives such a simple answer: “Lord God, you alone know.”

Maybe that is where I am today.

Life can be confusing. People are confusing. The systems we create can become so complicated that sometimes I look at them and wonder how any of it makes sense. There are days when I am incredibly grateful to God for everything I have, yet at the same time frustrated by the human condition and by the unfairness we sometimes encounter in this world.

And perhaps faith does not require me to pretend that I understand it.

Ezekiel didn't understand how a valley of dry bones could possibly live again. He simply acknowledged that God knew something he didn't.

Then I turned to Matthew, where the religious leaders are questioning and challenging Jesus. They have turned faith into arguments, rules, questions and complications. Finally Jesus is asked which commandment is the greatest.

His answer strips everything down to what matters: Love God with all your heart, soul and mind, and love your neighbor as yourself.

Maybe that is how these readings belong together after all.

When life becomes complicated, when people disappoint us, when circumstances seem unfair, and when we cannot understand what God could possibly be doing, perhaps we don't have to figure everything out.

We can simply say, **“Lord, You alone know.”**

Then we return to what Jesus told us to do.

Love God. Love one another.

And keep walking.

The valley Ezekiel saw looked completely finished. There wasn't even life left to save—only dry bones. Yet God was not finished with them.

That doesn't mean every disappointment will be corrected exactly as we want or every injustice will disappear. But it does remind me not to mistake what I can see today for the end of the story.

Maybe faith is not always understanding God. Sometimes faith is standing in the middle of something we do not understand and saying, **“Lord, I don't know what You are doing here, but You do.”**

And perhaps that is enough for today.

title: The Assumption of Mary: Putting Our Hand in Hers2
opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
body:
Today we celebrate the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary, the woman who believed before so many of us knew how to believe. Mary is our guide, the first among believers, and a mother whose heart would be pierced through her love for her Son and her witness to His suffering.

Everything began with her yes. When the angel came to Mary, she could not possibly have understood everything her answer would require of her. Yet she responded, "Behold, I am the handmaid of the Lord. May it be done to me according to your word." Through Mary's yes, Christ entered the world. Through her faith, she carried our Savior. Through her sorrow, she stood beneath the Cross as Jesus became our Redeemer.

And from that Cross, Jesus gave us something extraordinary. Seeing His mother and the disciple John, He said to Mary, "Woman, behold, your son." Then He said to John, "Behold, your mother." The Church has long understood John to represent more than one disciple standing beneath the Cross. In him, Christ entrusted Mary to His disciples—and His disciples to Mary.

But how do we actually draw close to her? How do we put our hand in the hand of a mother we cannot physically see? For some of us, even the word mother can be complicated. Our relationships with our earthly mothers may have been loving, difficult, imperfect, or some mixture of all three. Our own wounds and insecurities can affect the way we approach Mary. Perhaps we do not need to force that relationship. Perhaps we simply begin by saying, "Mary, I don't completely know how to come close to you. Teach me. Take my hand and bring me to your Son."

The Rosary helps us do exactly that. We repeat the Hail Mary so often that it can become easy to forget how powerful its words are. "Hail Mary, full of grace." These are the words of the angel Gabriel. "Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb." These are the words of Elizabeth. Then comes our request: "Holy Mary, Mother of God, pray for us sinners, now and at the hour of our death."

Now and at the hour of our death. Those words encompass our entire earthly existence. We ask Mary to pray for us now, in whatever we are facing, and someday when our earthly lives come to an end.

Throughout the centuries there have also been reported appearances of Mary. The Church approaches these carefully, and private revelations do not add anything necessary to the Gospel. Yet in the Marian apparitions the Church has recognized, the messages are remarkably consistent: pray, repent, return to God, seek peace, trust Christ, pray for others, and do not despair.

Mary's message ultimately remains the same one she gave at the wedding feast at Cana: "Do whatever He tells you." Perhaps that tells us everything we need to understand about devotion to Mary. She does not ask us to stop at her. She brings us to her Son.

On the Feast of her Assumption, we remember that Mary's life did not end with suffering. The woman who gave her body so that Christ could take on human flesh was brought, body and soul, into heavenly glory. She has already arrived where we hope one day to go. She is the mother who said yes, the mother whose heart was pierced, the mother who remained beneath the Cross, the disciple who believed, the woman full of grace, and the Queen of Heaven and Earth.

Maybe we don't have to understand perfectly how to have a relationship with her. Maybe we simply reach out our hand.

Mary, Mother of Jesus and our Mother, take our hands. Teach us your yes. Teach us to trust when we cannot understand what God is doing. Stay beside us in our sorrow. Pray for us in our weakness. And at the hour of our death, lead us to your Son, so that through Him we may see the Father and enter everlasting life. Amen.
